summary: For ages 11–12: build a number's prime factorisation with a factor tree, record it in index form (e.g. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5), and use prime factorisations to find HCF (lowest power of each shared prime) and LCM (highest power of each prime present). The conceptual anchor is the unique-factorisation property — however the tree is built, the multiset of primes is identical. A Venn diagram of two numbers' prime factors organises HCF (intersection product) and LCM (whole-diagram product). Includes production, reference/anchor, consolidation, and Socratic-discussion activities, with scaffold limits noted.
misconceptions: Thinking a number can have different prime factorisations depending on how the tree is drawn (missing the uniqueness property).
Treating 1 as prime, or including 1 in a factorisation.
Confusing HCF with LCM (taking the largest common multiple or smallest common factor), or muddling which is 'highest' vs 'lowest'.
Taking the highest index for HCF / lowest for LCM (rule reversed).
Stopping a factor tree at composite leaves (e.g. leaving 4 or 6 unfactored) so the factorisation isn't fully prime.

activities.title: Prime factory: build the tree, discover uniqueness
steps: Take a number such as 360 and repeatedly split it into a factor pair (e.g. 4 × 90), then keep splitting each branch until every leaf is a prime.
Collect the prime leaves and write them in index form: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
Now build 360 a second time starting from a different first split (e.g. 8 × 45 instead of 4 × 90). Record the prime leaves again.
Lay the two sets of prime leaves side by side and check: the trees branched differently, but the collected primes are identical (2³ × 3² × 5 both times).
Check each tree for composite leaves left unsplit (e.g. a 4 or a 9 that should become 2×2 or 3×3) and finish splitting them.
activities.insight: Every whole number greater than 1 has exactly one prime 'fingerprint': the order and shape of the splits do not change which primes (and how many of each) you end up with. Composite leaves must be fully broken down before the factorisation is complete.

activities.title: Venn organiser for HCF and LCM
steps: Write the prime factorisations of two numbers, e.g. 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3².
Place each number's prime factors (as individual copies) in a two-circle Venn diagram, putting the factor copies both numbers share in the overlap and the leftover copies in the outer regions.
Read the HCF as the product of the overlap (the shared primes, each taken at the lowest power both numbers have): 2² × 3 = 12.
Read the LCM as the product of the whole diagram (each prime at its highest power): 2³ × 3² = 72.
Check the relationship HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers: 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36.
Try a coprime pair such as 24 and 25 (24 = 2³ × 3, 25 = 5²): the overlap is empty, so HCF = 1 and LCM = 600.
activities.insight: A common factor can only be built from primes BOTH numbers have, taken at the lowest shared power — that is the HCF. The LCM must contain enough of every prime to be a multiple of both, so each prime appears at its highest power. The Venn regions are intended to make lowest-for-HCF / highest-for-LCM visible rather than a rule to memorise.

activities.title: Reference anchor: reveal the index form and the Venn result
steps: Study a completed factor tree for a number; before revealing, predict each leaf's prime value and the full index form.
Reveal the index form (e.g. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5) and compare with your prediction.
Study a two-number Venn of prime factors; predict the HCF (overlap) and LCM (whole diagram) before revealing them.
Reveal the HCF and LCM and check your reasoning about which powers went where.
activities.insight: A worked tree plus Venn serves as a clear reference for the layout of index form and the intersection/union logic of HCF and LCM.

activities.title: Consolidation checks
steps: Complete the missing indices: 360 = 2^□ × 3^□ × 5.
Find the HCF and LCM of 24 and 36 and state which is which.
Sort a set of numbers into prime vs composite (remembering 1 is neither).
Match each number to its correct prime factorisation.
activities.insight: Fluent recall of index form and correct HCF/LCM selection, with the prime/composite distinction secure.

activities.title: Socratic challenge: why is factorisation unique and why 1 isn't prime
steps: Respond to the question: 'Could 360 have a different set of prime factors if we split it a different way?' — justify your answer.
Explain why 1 is not counted as a prime, and what would go wrong with uniqueness if we allowed it.
Explain in your own words why taking shared primes at the lowest power gives the HCF, referring to what a common factor must divide.
activities.insight: Articulating the reasoning — common divisors are built only from shared primes, and every number is exactly one product of primes — is intended to cement the conceptual objective, not just the recipe.

checkQuestion: Find the highest common factor (HCF) of 24 and 36 using prime factorisation. Show your prime factors, then explain WHY taking the shared prime factors gives the HCF — why must that be the biggest number dividing both?
checkAnswer: 24 = 2³ × 3, 36 = 2² × 3²; the HCF takes the lowest power of each shared prime: 2² × 3 = 12. A child reasoning well explains that any common divisor can only be built from primes both numbers share, and taking the most of each shared prime that BOTH have gives the largest such divisor — resting on unique factorisation.
